title: How does ab change when a number goes down?
description: The four parts rule works for negative amounts too. Taking away two from one number while adding three to the other, and taking away three and four, are each expanded and checked with both numbers ten. Keeko doubts the sign of the last part.
teaching_notes: One idea: write a take away as adding a negative, then the four parts rule and the integer sign rules do the rest. Watch for students who give the last part a minus sign because both numbers are taken away.

source: Find how the product ab changes when (i) one number is decreased by 2 and the other increased by 3, (ii) one is decreased by 3 and the other by 4. Check each with a = 10, b = 10.
video_script.why: The child can expand when numbers grow. Here numbers also go down, and the signs must be kept right.
video_script.substitution: Write each take away as adding a negative, use the four parts rule, and check with both numbers ten.
video_script.anchor: the four parts rule with m and n shown as negative numbers
video_script.wrong_answer: the last part is minus twelve
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says negative three times negative four is minus twelve, so the last part is minus twelve. With eigh and b both ten, that gives eighteen, but seven times six is forty two.
video_script.payoff_line: The rules for multiplying integers fix every sign

final_answer.spoken: the first is eigh b plus three eigh minus two b minus six, and the second is eigh b minus four eigh minus three b plus twelve

never_show: a last part of minus twelve, marked as right
maths_rules: (a + m)(b + n) = ab + mb + an + mn holds for any integers m and n
a negative times a negative is positive
video_script.design: One idea: a take away is an add of a negative, and the four parts rule keeps the signs. Assumes the four parts rule. Wrong idea: the last part is minus twelve. The rule with its negative values stays through the idea and the doubt.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='block'/>Take two numbers, eigh and b, multiplied together.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How does the total change if one number goes down by two and the other up by three?
<bookmark mark='ask2'/>What if one goes down by three and the other goes down by four?

beats.on_screen: the two question tags stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the rule (a + m)(b + n) = ab + mb + an + mn; beside it a − 2 = a + (−2) and b − 4 = b + (−4)

marks.rule: the four parts rule is written with m and n
marks.neg: a − 2 = a + (−2) and b − 4 = b + (−4) are written beside it
marks.sign: the words signs come from integer rules appear

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>The four parts rule works when m and n are any integers.
<bookmark mark='neg'/>Taking away two is the same as adding negative two.
<bookmark mark='sign'/>Each part gets its sign from the rules for multiplying integers.

beats.on_screen: Given: (i) a − 2 and b + 3; (ii) a − 3 and b − 4
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, first case, eigh goes down by two and b goes up by three.
<bookmark mark='second'/>In the second case, eigh goes down by three and b goes down by four.

beats.on_screen: To find: the new products, checked with a = 10, b = 10

marks.find: the new products and the check are written as the things to find

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to expand both new products and check each with ten and ten.
<bookmark mark='mn'/>Step one, take the first case. Here m is negative two and n is three.
<bookmark mark='parts'/>The four parts are eigh b, negative two times b, eigh times three, and negative two times three.
<bookmark mark='tidy'/>That gives eigh b, plus three eigh, minus two b, minus six.
<bookmark mark='direct'/>Step two, check with eigh and b both ten. Eight times thirteen is one hundred four.
<bookmark mark='expr'/>The expression gives one hundred, plus thirty, minus twenty, minus six.
That is one hundred four too, so the two agree.
<bookmark mark='mn2'/>Step three, take the second case. Here m is negative three and n is negative four.
<bookmark mark='parts2'/>The last part is negative three times negative four.
Two negatives multiply to a positive, so that part is plus twelve.
<bookmark mark='tidy2'/>The result is eigh b, minus four eigh, minus three b, plus twelve.
<bookmark mark='direct2'/>Step four, check again with ten and ten. Seven times six is forty two.
<bookmark mark='expr2'/>The expression gives one hundred, minus forty, minus thirty, plus twelve.
That is forty two too.

marks.pay: the words the rules for multiplying integers fix every sign appear

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>The rules for multiplying integers fix every sign.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The first is eigh b plus three eigh minus two b minus six.
The second is eigh b minus four eigh minus three b plus twelve.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand next to the answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble shows (−3) × (−4) = −12 and ab − 4a − 3b − 12; the check shows 18 against 42; the bubble is crossed out and +12 replaces −12

marks.test: the check with 10 and 10 shows 18 against 42
marks.strike: the bubble is crossed out and +12 replaces −12

beats.colours: the wrong bubble in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the last part is minus twelve, because both signs are minus.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Try ten and ten. That gives one hundred, minus forty, minus thirty, minus twelve, which is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>But seven times six is forty two. A negative times a negative is positive, so the last part is plus twelve.
